messages.content: I want to build an incremental Java taint analyzer that preserves interprocedural soundness when edits change heap aliasing and virtual dispatch.

The central challenge is that a method-body edit can affect more than the method containing it. If it changes which references may point to the same heap object, or which implementation a virtual call may reach, the taint findings affected by that edit may extend across method boundaries. Incremental analysis must account for those effects rather than treating the edited body as an isolated unit.
How strong is the correctness requirement?

For Java without reflection or native calls, the incremental analyzer’s findings must equal the findings from sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. That is an equality requirement against the recomputation baseline, not merely a requirement that the incremental result remain sound in some broader sense.
So if the incremental result reports an extra finding, is that acceptable because it is conservative?

Not under the stated equality requirement. An extra finding would make its findings differ from those of the sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation, just as a missing finding would. The requirement is to match that baseline’s findings.
What does the context-sensitive part of the comparison mean here?

It specifies the kind of whole-program recomputation used as the reference. The incremental result is not being compared with an unspecified whole-program analysis or with a context-insensitive one. The node does not specify a particular way to represent contexts; it specifies the property of the recomputation whose findings must be matched.
Why call out heap aliasing separately from virtual dispatch?

They describe different ways an edit can alter interprocedural behavior. Heap aliasing concerns which references may denote the same objects, so a change can affect how information moves through reads and writes. Virtual dispatch concerns which method implementations a call may reach. Either kind of change can affect findings beyond the edited method.
Can you give me a general illustration without assuming a particular implementation?

Imagine a method-body edit changes which object a reference may denote. A later operation through another reference may then become relevant to a taint flow because the two references may alias. Separately, if an edit changes the possible receiver at a virtual call, the possible callee may change. Those are illustrations of why revisiting only the text of the edited method would not, by itself, establish agreement with whole-program recomputation.
Does preserving interprocedural soundness mean only following calls made directly by the edited method?

No such limit is stated. The requirement concerns findings after edits that change heap aliasing and virtual dispatch, compared with sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. A change may matter through relationships between methods, so the relevant question is whether the resulting findings match that recomputation, not whether an effect is one direct call away.
Is the target to discover only newly introduced findings?

The target is equality of findings after the edit. That covers both findings present in the recomputed result and findings absent from it. If an edit removes a flow in the recomputation baseline, retaining its former finding would also violate equality.
And what is the performance target?

Achieve at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. It is a median target for that suite, not a statement that every one of the 100 edits must individually achieve a 3× speedup.
Would a faster analysis that occasionally disagrees with recomputation satisfy the goal?

No. The speed target and the findings-equality requirement are both part of the goal. A speedup does not compensate for disagreement with sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation within the stated Java scope.
Does the goal say anything about results for reflection or native calls?

The stated findings-equality requirement is for Java without reflection or native calls. It does not specify the corresponding guarantee for programs that use either feature, so I would not infer one from this goal.
Am I right that the edits in the speed comparison are method-body edits, even though their effects might extend beyond a method body?

Yes. The performance comparison names a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. The edit location does not confine its possible effects: changes to aliasing or virtual dispatch can matter to interprocedural taint findings.
Does this specify how the analyzer should invalidate or reuse earlier work?

No particular invalidation, reuse, or analysis algorithm is specified. Those would be means of building an incremental analyzer; the stated requirements concern the findings it must produce and the median speedup it must achieve against full recomputation.
Then the important distinction is between doing less work and making fewer connections in the analysis?

Exactly as a statement of the objective: incremental execution is meant to improve performance, but the resulting findings must still equal those of sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. Doing less work cannot justify overlooking effects of an aliasing or dispatch change that alter those findings.
Does “at least 3× median speedup” establish that the analyzer is already that fast?
No. It states a target to achieve over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. It does not report a measured speedup or say the target has already been met.
I also don’t want the word “sound” to get blurred with “identical.” How would you keep those separate?

Soundness describes a correctness property of an analysis; identical findings describe agreement with a specified result. Here the reference is sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation, and the incremental analyzer must equal its findings for Java without reflection or native calls. Saying only that the incremental result is sound would not express the full requirement.
What should remain explicit when I state the goal in one sentence?

That it is an incremental Java taint analyzer; that edits changing heap aliasing and virtual dispatch must not break interprocedural soundness; that, for Java without reflection or native calls, its findings must equal sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation; and that it must achieve at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits.

For the incremental analyzer, I propose tracking derivation dependencies across context-sensitive taint, points-to, and dispatch summaries. When a method-body edit changes the analysis, retract affected facts and propagate additions to a fixed point.

That proposal treats the three kinds of summaries as connected rather than updating taint in isolation. A change in points-to information may affect dispatch or taint information; a dispatch change may affect which interprocedural taint information is relevant. Tracking derivation dependencies provides a way to identify facts that need reconsideration, while fixed-point propagation aims to carry additions through the connected analysis until no further additions follow.
What exactly is a derivation dependency in this proposal?

It is a record of what supports an analysis fact or summary result. If that support changes, the dependency indicates that the derived result may need to be revisited. The proposal calls for tracking such relationships across context-sensitive taint, points-to, and dispatch summaries, not just within each kind of summary separately.
Why does the tracking have to cross those summary boundaries?

Because those summaries can bear on one another. Possible points-to relationships can matter to heap-mediated taint flow and to possible virtual-call targets. Possible targets can, in turn, matter to interprocedural taint results. If dependencies stopped at a summary boundary, an edit could change information on one side without prompting reconsideration of a result derived on the other.
Does “context-sensitive” apply only to taint here?

The proposal says to track derivation dependencies across context-sensitive taint, points-to, and dispatch summaries. It does not spell out a representation for contexts or precisely assign a context-sensitivity scheme to each summary type. What matters in this statement is that dependency tracking respects the distinctions relevant to the context-sensitive analysis rather than treating all interprocedural results as interchangeable.
Suppose an edit removes a fact that helped justify a taint result. Is retracting that fact enough?

Not necessarily. The proposal calls for retracting affected facts, which includes reconsidering results that depend on changed support. Conceptually, a derived result should not remain solely because of a derivation that no longer holds. Conversely, removing one derivation does not by itself establish that the result has no other support. The proposal does not prescribe a particular mechanism for handling those cases.
So retraction is about support, not just deleting everything previously associated with the edited method?

Yes. Derivation dependencies are meant to focus reconsideration on facts affected by a change. That is different from assuming every fact associated with an edited method must disappear, and different from assuming that nothing outside that method can change. The proposal itself does not fix the granularity at which dependencies are recorded.
Where do additions fit after retraction?

An edit may make new facts derivable, including facts that become relevant through changed points-to or dispatch information. The proposed update therefore has both sides: retract affected facts whose prior support has changed, and propagate additions through the dependent analysis until a fixed point is reached. Addressing only removals would leave newly possible flows or targets unaccounted for.
Does reaching a fixed point mean a single pass through the summaries is enough?

No. “Propagate additions to a fixed point” means continuing while propagation produces further consequences. A newly derived fact may enable another derivation, including one in a different kind of summary. The proposal does not claim a single pass will suffice.
Can the dependency go from dispatch information back to points-to information, or is the direction fixed?

The proposal does not specify every allowed dependency direction. It says to track derivation dependencies across the three kinds of summaries. Any particular dependency should reflect an actual derivation in the analysis; it should not be assumed merely because two summary kinds exist. The important point is not to impose an artificial boundary that prevents an affected derivation from being revisited.
Could I describe this as keeping a record of why each relevant conclusion was reached?

That is a useful conceptual description of derivation tracking. The record connects conclusions to the information on which they depend, so that a changed premise can trigger reconsideration of affected conclusions. It does not, on its own, specify the storage format or how much detail to retain for each derivation.
And the conclusions can be in the taint, points-to, or dispatch part of the analysis?

Yes. The proposed dependency tracking spans context-sensitive taint, points-to, and dispatch summaries. That scope is central: an edit affecting heap aliasing or a possible virtual-call target should not be treated as unrelated to interprocedural taint findings simply because the immediate changed fact has a different label.
Does the proposal itself prove that incremental findings will equal whole-program recomputation?

No. It proposes an approach for maintaining the analysis under edits. The goal remains that, for Java without reflection or native calls, findings equal sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. Whether a particular realization of dependency tracking, retraction, and fixed-point propagation achieves that equality would have to be established; the proposal alone is not such a proof.
Nor does it imply the 3× median speedup has been measured?

Correct. Tracking affected derivations is an incremental strategy, not a reported performance result. The separate target is at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. This proposal does not state that the target has been reached.
Why include dispatch summaries if points-to summaries already describe possible receivers?

The proposal names dispatch summaries because the possible interprocedural calls matter in their own right to the taint analysis. Points-to information may help determine which targets are possible, but tracking the consequences of a target change still requires accounting for the dispatch results used by other derivations. The proposal does not require any particular division of information between the two summary types.
Could an edit both invalidate an old derivation and introduce a new one?

Yes; that is exactly why the proposed update includes retraction and addition propagation. A change need not be purely subtractive or purely additive. The analysis must account for affected prior support and for newly derivable consequences, including consequences that cross summary boundaries.
What does “affected” mean without a specified dependency representation?

At this level, it means facts whose derivations may be changed by the edit, directly or through other changed facts. The proposal identifies derivation dependencies as the basis for finding them, but does not commit to a particular representation or a precise update algorithm. Calling a fact affected is therefore about its connection to changed support, not merely its physical proximity to edited code.
I want to avoid claiming that fixed-point propagation repairs any possible omission in retraction. Is that fair?

Yes. Propagating additions to a fixed point addresses consequences that can be derived from the updated information. It does not make an incorrectly retained, unsupported fact acceptable. Both sides of the proposal matter: reconsider and retract affected facts as appropriate, then propagate additions until the update stabilizes.
If a fact has more than one reason to hold, would removing one reason automatically retract it?

Not as a matter of the proposal’s meaning. An affected fact needs reconsideration when a supporting derivation changes; it should not be treated as unsupported if another valid derivation still supports it. This is a conceptual distinction between withdrawing a derivation and withdrawing the fact it supported, not a commitment to a particular bookkeeping technique.
Can you state the proposal compactly without turning it into a completed implementation?

Track derivation dependencies across context-sensitive taint, points-to, and dispatch summaries so method-body edits can trigger reconsideration and retraction of affected facts; then propagate newly derivable facts to a fixed point. That states the proposed approach without claiming it has already been implemented, proven equivalent to recomputation, or shown to meet the speed target.
How can provenance identify every virtual call edge invalidated by changed receiver points-to sets without rescanning unaffected contexts?

Conceptually, provenance must connect each virtual call edge to the receiver points-to information that justifies it, while retaining the relevant calling context. When a receiver’s points-to information changes, the analysis can follow those dependency links to candidate edges and reconsider their support. Contexts with no dependency on the changed information need not be rescanned merely because the edit occurred elsewhere. That describes the required relationship, not a completed implementation or proof that every dependency has been captured.
Why retain the calling context in that relationship?

Because the proposed analysis is context-sensitive. A receiver at the same call site may have different relevant points-to information in different contexts. Provenance that loses that distinction could either overlook an affected edge or needlessly revisit edges in contexts whose receiver information did not change.
Is a dependency from a points-to set to a call edge enough?

Only if it is precise enough to answer which edge derivations relied on which receiver information. A coarse link might safely identify candidates, but could require revisiting more contexts than necessary. More importantly, missing a genuine link would make it possible to leave an invalid edge untouched. The proposal does not fix the granularity of those links.
What if the points-to set changes but the set of possible call targets does not?

The change may warrant reconsidering dependent derivations, but it does not follow that a call edge must be removed. The question is whether each edge remains justified under the updated receiver information. A changed input and an invalidated edge are not the same thing.
So provenance identifies edges to check, rather than declaring that all of them are invalid?

Yes. Following dependencies identifies potentially affected edges. Reconsidering their support determines whether each remains, must be retracted, or whether changed receiver information enables an addition. That distinction matters when several receiver possibilities can justify the same edge.
Can you illustrate the multiple-support issue in general terms?

Suppose two possible receiver objects both justify reaching the same implementation at a virtual call. If one possibility disappears but the other remains, a derivation has been lost, yet the call edge can still be justified. If the removed possibility was its only support, the edge may need retraction. The example illustrates why provenance needs to account for support, not simply label an edge as touched.
How would it find a newly possible edge? There cannot be an old edge to trace backward from.

That is the other side of the update. Existing derivation dependencies can identify edges whose old support may have changed; newly available receiver information must also be propagated forward to determine whether it justifies new dispatch results. Tracking retractions alone would not find an edge that did not previously exist.
Does avoiding rescans of unaffected contexts mean never looking beyond the context where the receiver set first changed?

No. A changed result may feed a derivation in another context, including an interprocedural result. Avoiding unaffected contexts means following actual dependencies instead of scanning every context indiscriminately. Any context reached through an affected derivation still needs appropriate reconsideration.
What would make the claim that every invalidated edge is identified credible?

The crucial condition is complete dependency coverage: every edge whose validity depends on changed receiver points-to information must be reachable through the recorded provenance, either directly or through intermediate affected facts. Retraction must also respect any remaining support. Without establishing that coverage, avoiding a broad rescan could miss an invalidated edge. The question raises that obligation; it does not state that it has already been met.
Could the provenance connect through summaries rather than directly from a receiver fact to every edge?

Conceptually, yes. A dependency path could pass through a points-to or dispatch summary, provided following it still reaches every edge whose support changed and preserves the distinctions needed for context sensitivity. The requirement is about complete, usable derivation relationships, not a specified direct-link format.
If the receiver information loses an object, is every edge associated with that object invalidated?

Not automatically. Losing that receiver possibility withdraws support associated with it, but an edge may still have another valid justification. Provenance should lead the analysis to reconsider the edge; the updated supports determine whether it remains. Conversely, an edge whose sole justification disappears must not be retained simply because it was previously reported.
What if a context’s points-to information has not changed, but an upstream dependency has?

The relevant distinction is whether the derivations used by that context are affected, not just whether a locally displayed set has changed at one moment. If following an upstream change can alter the receiver information or a dispatch result used there, that context is not unaffected. If its relevant inputs and derivations remain unchanged, rescanning it would not be required by this dependency-based approach.
Does the question assume a particular way to store provenance?

No. It asks how provenance can provide complete identification without rescanning unaffected contexts; it does not prescribe a data structure. One can discuss the necessary property—being able to trace from changed, context-relevant receiver information to every dependent edge—without claiming a particular representation has been chosen.
Where does the fixed point from the proposal enter this question?

After changed receiver information leads to retractions or additions in dispatch results, those changes may have further consequences in the connected analysis. Propagation to a fixed point addresses such follow-on additions. It does not replace the need to identify and reconsider all edges whose previous support has been invalidated.
I’m trying to distinguish not rescanning unaffected contexts from assuming that only directly connected edges can change.

They are different. Avoiding a rescan means using provenance to follow the consequences of a change. A dependency path can have intermediate summaries or derivations, so an edge need not be directly connected to the initially changed fact to be affected. An unaffected context is one outside the relevant dependency consequences, not merely one outside the edited method.
And this is still an open question about the proposal, rather than evidence that it already works?

Yes. The question asks whether provenance can be complete enough to catch every virtual call edge invalidated by changed receiver points-to sets while avoiding scans of unaffected contexts. Explaining the needed dependency coverage and support checks does not establish that a particular analyzer achieves them, matches whole-program recomputation, or meets the 3× median speedup target.
My hypothesis is that reverse-indexed receiver points-to justifications can identify all affected context-qualified call edges without rescanning contexts lacking changed receivers.

That proposes a specific way to answer the provenance question: start from receiver points-to justifications that changed and use a reverse index to find the context-qualified call edges that depend on them. The claim has two parts: it would find every affected edge, and it would avoid rescanning contexts whose receivers have not changed. Both parts remain hypotheses, not established results.
What does “reverse-indexed” add to the idea of recording provenance?

It emphasizes the direction of lookup. Rather than inspecting call edges one by one to ask what supports each, the analysis would be able to start with a changed receiver points-to justification and find the edges associated with that justification. The node does not specify the index’s representation or maintenance procedure.
Why say “justifications” rather than simply “points-to sets”?

A set tells you which receiver possibilities are present; justifications concern why those possibilities are present and which call-edge derivations depend on them. That distinction matters when a change removes one basis for an edge but another basis may still remain. The hypothesis is about indexing those relationships, not merely noticing that a set’s contents changed.
And what makes a call edge context-qualified?

It means the edge is distinguished by the relevant analysis context, rather than identified solely by a call site and possible target. The hypothesis specifically claims to find affected edges at that context-qualified level. It does not prescribe a particular context representation.
If the same virtual call appears in two contexts, does this hypothesis say both have to be rescanned when only one receiver changes?

No. Its proposed selectivity is precisely that a context lacking a changed receiver would not be rescanned on that basis. The changed receiver’s reverse-indexed justifications would identify the affected context-qualified edges. Whether an actual index achieves that separation is part of what the hypothesis would need to establish.
Does “all affected” mean every edge the lookup returns must be removed?

No. An affected edge is one whose justification needs reconsideration; it is not necessarily an invalid edge. If support changes but the edge remains justified, it can remain. The completeness claim is that no edge requiring such reconsideration is missed.
How does the hypothesis relate to the case where one receiver possibility disappears but another still supports the same target?

The lost justification could lead through the reverse index to the relevant context-qualified edge, marking it for reconsideration. The edge would not have to disappear if another justification still supports it. This illustrates what the index is intended to locate, without claiming a particular scheme for maintaining multiple supports.
Could a changed receiver also make a new virtual call edge possible?

Yes, a changed receiver points-to set can include an addition as well as a removal. The hypothesis says changed receiver justifications identify all affected context-qualified call edges; it should therefore be read as addressing edges affected by changed receiver information, not only old edges that might be retracted. It does not, by itself, specify the full procedure for deriving newly possible edges.
Is it fair to say that the reverse index avoids checking every context just to discover whether its receiver changed?

That is the proposed benefit. If changed receiver justifications can be used to reach their dependent, context-qualified edges, contexts lacking changed receivers need not be rescanned merely to look for affected edges. The hypothesis does not supply measurements of how much work that saves.
What would have to be true for the word “all” to hold?

Every call edge affected by a receiver points-to change would have to be reachable through the indexed justifications for that change, with its context distinction preserved. An omitted dependency could cause an affected edge to be missed; an imprecise dependency could cause extra reconsideration. The hypothesis asserts the desired coverage but does not demonstrate it.
Could an edge be reached through more than one changed justification?

Conceptually, yes: different receiver possibilities or derivations could point to the same context-qualified edge. Reaching an edge more than once would not mean it has to be retracted more than once, and losing one justification would not prove that every justification is gone. Those are consequences to account for when interpreting the hypothesis, not specified implementation decisions.
Does the phrase “contexts lacking changed receivers” mean contexts with unchanged call edges?

Not exactly. It refers to contexts in which the relevant receiver information has not changed; the hypothesis says those contexts need not be rescanned. An edge’s status is a separate question. The proposed index is meant to connect receiver changes to edges requiring attention without equating a changed receiver with an invalidated edge.
Could I strengthen the claim to say no other analysis work is needed in those contexts?

That would go beyond this hypothesis. It specifically concerns identifying affected context-qualified call edges without rescanning contexts lacking changed receivers. It does not rule out other analysis work for other reasons, or make a general claim that such contexts can never be involved in any subsequent analysis.
Does this settle whether the incremental taint analyzer matches whole-program recomputation?

No. Complete identification of call edges affected by receiver changes would address one important part of maintaining dispatch information. The broader findings-equality requirement also concerns the connected taint and points-to analysis. The hypothesis does not assert that the complete analyzer has been proved equivalent to sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation.
Nor should I present it as an observed speedup?

Right. Avoiding rescans of contexts lacking changed receivers is a proposed way to limit work; it is not a measured performance result. In particular, this hypothesis does not say that the goal of at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits has been achieved.
Can you phrase the hypothesis so its selectivity and completeness are both unmistakable?

Reverse-indexed receiver points-to justifications are hypothesized to locate every call edge affected by a receiver change at the appropriate context-qualified granularity, while avoiding rescans of contexts whose receivers have not changed. “Every” expresses the proposed completeness; the restriction on rescans expresses the proposed selectivity. Neither is yet a demonstrated outcome.

I want to turn the receiver-provenance idea into a plan: implement receiver-fact reverse indexes, update dispatch edges on points-to deltas, and compare context-qualified targets against full recomputation on 100 edits.

That plan has three connected parts. The reverse indexes would make it possible to find dispatch derivations associated with changed receiver facts. Updating dispatch edges on points-to deltas would then account for receiver possibilities that were removed or added. Finally, comparing context-qualified targets against full recomputation on 100 edits would check whether the incremental dispatch results agree with that baseline in the cases examined. These are planned activities, not reported implementation or comparison results.
What is a receiver-fact reverse index meant to let me look up?

It is meant to let you start with a receiver fact and find the dispatch information derived from it, rather than start with every dispatch edge and inspect its receiver information. The relevant context must remain distinguishable because the planned comparison concerns context-qualified targets. The plan does not specify an index representation.
Is the reverse index itself the evidence that no affected edge will be missed?

No. Implementing an index creates a way to follow recorded relationships; completeness depends on whether every relevant receiver-fact justification is actually represented and followed. The proposed comparison against full recomputation can examine the resulting targets on 100 edits, but the plan does not claim that the index has already been shown complete.
Why update on points-to deltas instead of just noting that a method body changed?

A points-to delta identifies a change in receiver possibilities relevant to dispatch. The plan uses those changes to focus dispatch updates, rather than treating every method-body edit as a reason to revisit all contexts. That is the intended connection between the reverse index and the dispatch update, not a claim that every edit necessarily changes a receiver.
Does a delta include both things disappearing and things becoming possible?

Yes, in the ordinary sense of a change between points-to results. Removed receiver possibilities may withdraw support for existing dispatch edges; added possibilities may justify new ones. The plan says to update dispatch edges on points-to deltas, without spelling out a particular update procedure for either direction.
If a receiver fact disappears, would the corresponding dispatch edge always be deleted?

Not necessarily. The lost fact may be one of several justifications for the same edge. Updating the edge means reconsidering whether it still has support under the changed points-to information, not automatically deleting it because one receiver fact was removed.
And if a receiver fact appears, the plan should account for a target that was not previously present?

Yes. Updating dispatch edges on points-to deltas encompasses considering additions that make a target newly possible. The plan does not state that every added receiver fact yields a new target; different receiver possibilities can lead to an already-present target.
What exactly am I comparing after the updates?

Context-qualified targets: the possible virtual-call targets distinguished by their relevant analysis contexts. The comparison is between the incrementally updated targets and those obtained by full recomputation on 100 edits. It is more specific than simply asking whether the overall number of targets matches.
Why wouldn't matching totals be enough?

Two results can have the same total count yet disagree about which target belongs to which context. Comparing context-qualified targets addresses the identities of the targets in their contexts, which is what matters to this dispatch-focused plan.
Does the plan say to compare just one selected call site per edit?

No such selection is stated. It says to compare context-qualified targets against full recomputation on 100 edits. I would not add a restriction to one call site, or claim a more detailed comparison procedure, without specifying it separately.
Is the number 100 a performance measurement here?

No. Here, 100 is the number of edits for the planned target comparison. The comparison is about context-qualified dispatch targets. The broader goal also includes a median speedup requirement, but this plan does not report timings or say that the speedup has been measured.
How does this plan address the question about not rescanning unaffected contexts?

The intended route is to use receiver-fact reverse indexes to find dispatch information associated with changed receiver facts, then update edges from the points-to deltas. That would avoid making a scan of every context the default way to discover affected edges. The plan does not yet establish that all unaffected contexts are avoided in an implementation, or that every affected edge is found.
Would the comparison against full recomputation show whether the updates were correct?

It would provide a direct check of the context-qualified targets on the 100 edits being compared. Agreement there would be evidence about those comparisons; disagreement would expose a difference to investigate. The plan itself contains no comparison outcome, and agreement on those edits would not by itself prove correctness for every possible edit.
Does comparing dispatch targets also establish equality of taint findings?

Not on its own. Dispatch targets are one component relevant to the incremental taint analyzer. The larger goal requires findings to equal sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls. This plan specifically calls for comparing context-qualified targets, not for reporting a comparison of all taint findings.
Could the index be used for an unchanged receiver fact in a context anyway?

The plan is to update dispatch edges on points-to deltas, so the intended starting point is changed receiver information. It does not specify every circumstance in which an implementation might consult an index. What it avoids claiming is that every context must be rescanned merely to find out whether its receiver contributed to a changed dispatch result.
What if a points-to delta reaches an edge that remains valid?

That is compatible with the plan. The reverse index can identify an edge for reconsideration because one of its receiver-fact justifications changed, while the updated dispatch result still retains that edge. The comparison should concern the resulting context-qualified targets, not whether every visited edge changed status.
I don't want to conflate indexing changed receiver facts with a guarantee that the index is precise.

That's an important distinction. An index might return extra edges for reconsideration and still allow correct results, though it would do more work. Missing an affected edge is a different concern because it could leave the incremental target set out of agreement with full recomputation. Implementing receiver-fact reverse indexes is the plan; their completeness and selectivity are not yet established outcomes.
What should I avoid claiming when I describe the 100-edit comparison?

Avoid saying that it has already been run, that the context-qualified targets matched, that all invalidated call edges were identified, or that a speedup was achieved. The current statement is a plan to compare incrementally updated context-qualified targets with full recomputation on 100 edits.
Can you give me a concise formulation of the plan that keeps the order clear?

Implement receiver-fact reverse indexes; use points-to deltas to update dispatch edges; then compare the resulting context-qualified targets with full recomputation on 100 edits. That preserves the planned sequence without treating the proposed mechanism or its evaluation as a completed result.
I’m instrumenting DispatchDelta-100 to compare reverse-indexed dispatch updates against full recomputation and count unaffected contexts rescanned after 100 method-body edits.

That gives DispatchDelta-100 two observations to make over the 100 method-body edits: whether the incrementally updated dispatch results agree with full recomputation, and how often contexts unaffected by the relevant changes are nevertheless rescanned. The comparison examines the dispatch-update result; the count examines whether the update avoids work outside the affected contexts. Instrumenting those observations does not yet report either outcome.
What should the comparison be understood to cover?

It compares dispatch results produced by reverse-indexed updates with results from full recomputation after the edits. In the receiver-provenance plan, the results of interest are context-qualified targets, so agreement means more than obtaining the same total number of call edges: the target in each relevant context matters.
And why count unaffected contexts rescanned separately?

Matching full recomputation would speak to the dispatch result, but not to whether the reverse index avoids unnecessary rescans. Conversely, a low rescan count would not show that every affected edge was handled correctly. The two observations address distinct parts of the proposed approach.
Does “unaffected” mean any context that happens not to contain the edited method?

No. A method-body edit can change receiver information used elsewhere. For this activity, the important distinction is whether a context is affected by the receiver changes relevant to the dispatch update, not whether it contains the edited text. The count should not classify a context as unaffected solely because it is in another method.
The hypothesis specifically mentioned contexts lacking changed receivers. Is that the connection?

Yes. Counting unaffected contexts rescanned lets the activity examine the proposed selectivity of reverse-indexed receiver justifications: can dispatch updates proceed without rescanning contexts whose receivers did not change? The count is an observation to collect, not an assertion that the number will be zero.
If the incremental targets match full recomputation, can I say the index avoided rescanning unaffected contexts?
Not from that comparison alone. The results might match even if the updater rescanned many unaffected contexts. That is why DispatchDelta-100 also counts those rescans.
If the count is zero, does that establish that the dispatch updates are complete?

No. Avoiding rescans is a selectivity property; completeness concerns finding every affected context-qualified call edge. An updater could avoid unaffected contexts and still miss an affected one. Comparison with full recomputation is the separate check on the resulting dispatch targets for the 100 edits.
What does the full-recomputation side contribute that the reverse index cannot establish by itself?

It provides an independently recomputed result to compare with the incremental dispatch update. The reverse index says where the updater looked; the comparison checks what targets it ultimately produced. The activity does not say that this comparison has already been performed or that the results agree.
Would simply counting how many contexts the updater visited answer the rescan question?

Not by itself. The activity calls for counting *unaffected contexts rescanned*. A total visit count would not distinguish work on contexts reached because of relevant changes from rescans of contexts outside those changes. I’d like to explore another proposal for the incremental Java taint analyzer: partition context-sensitive call and heap dependencies into strongly connected components, or SCCs. After an edit, recompute affected closures while reusing untouched summaries.

This proposal uses dependency structure to separate work that may need recomputation from summaries that can remain in use. An SCC groups dependency nodes that are mutually reachable, so changes within such a group may need to be considered together. The important qualification is “affected closures”: recomputation cannot stop at the edited method or even necessarily at its SCC if consequences extend through call or heap dependencies.
What does it mean to partition the dependencies into SCCs?

In general graph terms, an SCC is a maximal group of nodes where each node can reach every other through directed dependencies. Partitioning means assigning the relevant context-sensitive call and heap dependencies to those groups. The proposal does not specify what an individual graph node represents or how the partition is stored.
Why include heap dependencies as well as calls?

A method-body edit that changes heap aliasing can affect taint flow beyond a direct call relationship. If the partition represented only calls, it could fail to express dependencies arising through shared heap information. The proposal therefore includes both context-sensitive call and heap dependencies in the structure used to identify affected work.
Does “context-sensitive” mean an SCC is just a group of methods?

Not necessarily. A plain method-level grouping could lose distinctions between different contexts of analysis. The proposal calls for partitioning *context-sensitive* dependencies, while leaving the exact representation of contexts and graph nodes unspecified. Whatever representation is used must preserve distinctions that matter to the recomputation baseline.
Why group mutually dependent parts together?

Within a dependency cycle, a change to one part can feed back into another part of the same group. Treating the group as a unit provides a way to account for that mutual dependence. SCCs also make dependencies between groups easier to discuss: once each SCC is treated as a group, the directed graph between those groups has no cycles.
Does that mean every SCC has to be recomputed after every edit?

No. The proposal is specifically to recompute *affected closures* and reuse untouched summaries. An SCC outside the consequences of an edit need not be recomputed merely because an edit occurred elsewhere, provided its summary really remains untouched by the relevant changes.
What is an affected closure in this setting?

Conceptually, it is the connected scope of analysis work that must be reconsidered after an edit, following the dependencies through which that edit can affect results. Calling it a closure emphasizes that work may extend beyond the first SCC reached. The proposal does not supply an exact traversal rule or a fixed boundary for every edit.
Could the closure be just the SCC containing the edited body?

It could be limited to that SCC only if no relevant consequences pass beyond it. As a general rule, the proposal cannot assume that boundary: changed call or heap information may affect dependent summaries in other SCCs. The affected closure has to account for such propagation.
What does reusing an untouched summary actually claim?

It means retaining a summary whose relevant inputs and derivations have not been affected, rather than recomputing it unnecessarily. “Untouched” must be justified by the dependency relationships; it cannot simply mean that the summary belongs to a method whose source text was not edited.
A method might be unedited but still be affected through the heap, then?

Yes. Heap aliasing can connect the consequences of an edit to analysis results elsewhere. That is why the proposal tracks heap dependencies as well as calls, and why the criterion for reuse is whether a summary is unaffected—not whether its own method body changed.
How does virtual dispatch fit into the call side?

A change in possible virtual-call targets can change interprocedural dependencies. The call portion of this proposal must be able to reflect the context-sensitive calls relevant after an edit. The proposal does not specify how virtual targets are computed or how changes to them are represented.
Could an edit change the SCC partition itself?

Conceptually, yes. If an edit changes relevant call or heap dependencies, the graph whose SCCs are being used may also change. A sound use of the proposal cannot simply assume that a partition based on earlier dependencies always describes the dependencies after the edit. The node does not prescribe how to maintain or rebuild that partition.
So I shouldn’t say SCC membership is fixed for the lifetime of the analyzer?

Correct. Fixed membership is not part of this proposal. The SCCs are a way of organizing context-sensitive call and heap dependencies, and those dependencies may change under the edits the analyzer is intended to handle.
Would an added dependency and a removed dependency raise different concerns?

Both can change which results depend on which others. An added dependency may bring analysis work into an affected closure; a removed one may change what remains justified or how parts of the dependency graph are grouped. The proposal says to recompute affected closures after edits, without committing to separate procedures for those two cases.
If a dependency disappears, could I immediately reuse everything outside its former SCC?

That would be too strong without checking consequences. A disappearing dependency may change results that were derived through it, and those results may have dependents beyond the former SCC. The proposed boundary is the affected closure as determined by relevant dependencies, not a blanket rule based on former SCC membership.
Does recomputing an affected closure imply doing a whole-program recomputation for that closure?

It means recomputing the analysis results that the proposal identifies as affected, while reusing summaries outside that scope. The proposal does not specify the internal recomputation algorithm, how an SCC is solved, or how much of a summary is recalculated.

A reused summary must still be valid for the edited program in its relevant context. If an edit changes a call or heap dependency on which that summary relies, treating it as untouched could cause the incremental findings to differ from sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. The proposal identifies reuse as an approach; it does not itself prove that the boundary between affected and untouched summaries is always correct.

No. SCCs organize dependencies; they do not independently guarantee that every relevant dependency was represented or every affected result recomputed. The required outcome remains equality of taint findings with sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls.

It could reduce work yet still be incorrect if an affected summary were mistakenly reused. Performance and findings equality must be evaluated separately. This proposal asserts neither a measured speedup nor completed correctness verification.

Reusing untouched summaries is the proposed way to avoid some full-program work. Whether that yields at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits is an empirical question; the proposal gives no timing result.

A separate group with no relevant dependency path from the change could retain its summary. That illustrates the proposed distinction without fixing a particular graph construction or claiming the boundary has been demonstrated.

Missing an indirect dependency. A summary can look locally unchanged while its justification depends on altered heap information or a changed possible call. To reuse it consistently with the goal, the affected-closure calculation must account for those interprocedural paths.

That states the proposed method without claiming that its closure boundaries have been proved sound or that it has achieved the ≥3× median speedup target.
